allCourses.title: Advanced Academic Writing Across the Curriculum
allCourses.restriction: Restricted to students whose first language is not English.
allCourses.description: Designed for transfer students who speak English as a second language. Focuses on developing academic reading and writing skills including essay content, organization, vocabulary, and grammar. Academic content also covered.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.

allCourses.title: Oral English Communication I
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Designed to help students hear and produce the sounds of English as an International Language with greater accuracy and confidence. Focuses on pronunciation features (e.g., consonant sounds, consonant clusters, vowels, thought groups, and nuclear stress).
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Oral English Communication II
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Designed to help students develop conversational fluency in English as an International Language. Focuses on applying knowledge of linguistic features and communicative skills during conversational exchange in a variety of social, academic, and professional contexts.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Oral English Communication III
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Designed to help students hone their public speaking skills in English as an International Language. Focuses on preparing, organizing, and delivering speeches and presentations and interacting with the audience, emphasizing skills needed in academic settings.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Academic Writing
allCourses.description: Grammar, sentence structure, paragraph and essay organization of formal written English.

allCourses.title: Academic Writing
allCourses.description: Grammar, sentence structure, paragraph and essay organization of formal written English.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( AC ENG 20A OR PLACEMENT EXAM or authorization )

allCourses.title: Essentials of Academic Writing
allCourses.description: Grammar, sentence structure, paragraph and essay organization of formal written English.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( AC ENG 20B OR PLACEMENT EXAM or authorization )

allCourses.title: Academic Writing
allCourses.description: Grammar, sentence structure, paragraph and essay organization of formal written English.

allCourses.title: Introduction to Graduate Research Writing
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Designed to introduce key components and skills for successful graduate-level academic writing. Topics cover summarizing and synthesizing sources, understanding appropriate source use conventions, developing and organizing ideas for research writing, revising, and editing.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Graduate Writing for Scholarly Publication
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Designed to help graduate students in the preparation of a conference paper or journal manuscript for publication. Topics cover writing for academic publication in their fields and understanding disciplinary source use conventions.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Thesis/Dissertation Writing for Graduate Students
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Designed to help graduate students in the preparation of a thesis/dissertation (or proposal). Topics cover planning a thesis/dissertation project, understanding the focuses and goals of different chapters, and practicing different ways of integrating sources to avoid plagiarism.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Academic English Reading and Vocabulary
allCourses.description: Intensive reading exercises with occasional practice in extensive reading, focusing on comprehension, development of vocabulary, syntax, rhetorical features, reading strategies, and study skills.

allCourses.title: ESL Reading and Vocabulary
allCourses.description: Extensive reading and discussion with emphasis on journal articles, textbook chapters, notetaking, and the interpretation of charts, diagrams, tables, and figures.

allCourses.title: Oral English Communication I
allCourses.description: Designed to help students hear and produce the sounds of English as an International Language with greater accuracy and confidence. Focuses on pronunciation features (e.g., consonant sounds, consonant clusters, vowels, thought groups, and nuclear stress).
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Oral English Communication II
allCourses.description: Designed to help students develop conversational fluency in English as an International Language. Focuses on applying knowledge of linguistic features and communicative skills during conversational exchange in a variety of social, academic, and professional contexts.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Oral English Communication III
allCourses.description: Designed to help students hone their public speaking skills in English as an International Language. Focuses on preparing, organizing, and delivering speeches and presentations and interacting with the audience, emphasizing skills needed in academic settings.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: ESL International TA Workshop
allCourses.description: Designed for advanced-level international students preparing to be teaching assistants. Provides extensive practice in oral and written communication skills associated with teaching introductory-level college courses and participating in academic presentations and discussions. Review and analysis of language problems.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: AC ENG 23A or AC ENG 23B or AC ENG 23C
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Grammar
allCourses.description: A full review of English grammar covering the following areas: grammar terms, verb tenses, verb forms, conditionals, passive and word forms, punctuation, sentence structure. The concepts are applied in targeted sentence and paragraph writing practice.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Special Topics in ESL
allCourses.description: Directed and individualized work in English as a second language not covered in the AC ENG 20, 21, 22 sequence.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Modern African American Art
allCourses.description: Investigates the history of modern African American art; emphasis on the politics of representation. Examines art in a variety of media from material culture and textiles to painting and photography. Issues of migration, nationalism, gender, sexuality, and hybridity are discussed.

allCourses.title: Contemporary African American Art
allCourses.description: Investigates the history of contemporary African American art; emphasis on the politics of representation. Explores art in a variety of media: painting, sculpture, photography, installation, and new media. Cultural politics, appropriation, identity, gender, sexuality, hybridity and civil rights issues discussed.

allCourses.title: Early African American Literature
allCourses.description: Examines the earliest forms of black literary practices, including the jeremiad, the slave narrative, the pamphlet, poetry, the short story, and how these literary forms are related to the historical experiences of enslavement and emancipation.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: African American Literature 1900-Present
allCourses.description: Examines individual literary forms and/or authors, as well as movements such as the Harlem Renaissance and the Black Arts Movement. Explores how black literary practices represent the conditions of modern subjectivities and environments.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: African American Cinema and Media
allCourses.description: Explores the diversity of Black creative production and the historical, social, and economic forces that shaped their emergence. May include Black film, hip-hop culture, fine art, photography, and others.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: International Cultures
allCourses.description: Explores the various cultures of the African diaspora and their impacts on a global scale. Examines a diverse range of media, including music (reggae, hip-hop), literature, film, and others and the links between culture and social movements throughout the diaspora.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Race and Visual Representation
allCourses.description: Examines film, documentary, fine art, photography, and other visual media to explore the multiple ways in which ideas about race are projected and woven through the visual landscape and the impacts this has on perpetuating social inequalities.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Topics in African American Humanities
allCourses.description: Provides students with an opportunity to pursue advanced work in African American studies from one or more humanities approaches (literature, film and media studies, art history, and others).
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: African American Women in Art
allCourses.description: Examines depictions of and by African American women in art and popular culture through a variety of media including textiles, painting, sculpture, photography, and installation. Focuses on African American women's experiences, perspectives, and strategies for contemporary representation.

allCourses.title: Topics in Gender/Sexuality
allCourses.description: Expressions of genders and sexualities across the spectrum of African American experience and creativity.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Caribbean History: Colonization to Emancipation
allCourses.description: Exploration of the history of the archipelago from pre-Columbian times to the end of slavery; examining the impact of European colonization, decimation of the indigenous populations, African slavery, resistance, and emancipation; the unity and diversity of experience in region.

allCourses.title: Caribbean History: Emancipation to Independence
allCourses.description: Post-emancipation and anti-colonial struggles ending with political independence for most of the region. Examines social, political, economic, cultural dimensions of post-emancipation period, including large-scale migration to Central America, the U.S., and Britain; the region's global cultural and political contribution.

allCourses.title: History of the African Diaspora
allCourses.description: Examines the causes and consequences of the multiple diasporas of African peoples since the sixteenth century in the Atlantic world, especially the Americas and Europe.

allCourses.title: Topics in African American History
allCourses.description: Studies in selected areas of African American history.  Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Topics in African American Music
allCourses.description: Examines African American musical forms and traditions, such as blues, jazz, and reggae, in performance and/or critical and theoretical contexts.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Topics in Expressive Forms
allCourses.description: Examines various forms of aesthetic expression in the African diaspora, including dance, music, and the plastic arts, as well as artistic visions of black cyberspace, digital activism, film, video, and aesthetic conceptions of the future.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: African Americans and Photography
allCourses.description: Explores depictions of and by African Americans through photography. Examines the history of photography in relationship to African American culture through a variety of media from early daguerreotype processes to digital imagery.

allCourses.title: Comparative Minority Politics
allCourses.description: Examines the political experiences of Blacks, Latinos, and Asian Americans in the United States from roughly 1950 to the present. Focuses on how each group has pursued political empowerment via both conventional political channels and social movements.

allCourses.title: African American Politics
allCourses.description: Examines politics of African Americans in order to gain a broader perspective of the American political process. Major developments in African American politics (including the civil rights movement, Black presidential bids), continuing problem of racism, responsiveness of key governing institutions.

allCourses.title: African American Psychology
allCourses.description: Historical overview of the development of black psychology and the African American frame of reference. Topics include personality development, psychological assessment, issues in education, black mental health, and the role of the African American psychologist in the community.

allCourses.title: African American Social Formations
allCourses.description: Topics which promote critical investigation into the historical, political, and social formations associated with the Black Diaspora.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Intercultural Studies
allCourses.description: Studies relationships between various cultural formations within the Black Diaspora and the exchange, amalgamations, and tensions between Black Diasporic formations and non-Black formations. Examines expressions of racialization as representation, adaption, and resistance.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: African Societies and Politics
allCourses.description: Examines the violent incorporation of Africa within European modernity. Places the discourse of Pan-Africanism, African Nationalisms, Negritude, African Marxism, and/or African Socialism in juxtaposition to the forces of capitalism, colonialism, and imperialism that restructure African history.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Critical Race Theory
allCourses.restriction: Upper-division students only. African-American Studies Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Criminology, Law and Society Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Social Ecology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Introduction to Critical Race Theory and key American cases on racial inequality. Using this literature, examines the possibilities and pitfalls of legal claims of race, gender, and sexuality discrimination in the age of colorblindness.

allCourses.title: Topics in African American Social Sciences
allCourses.description: Provides students with an opportunity to pursue advanced work in African American studies from one or more social science approaches (psychology, sociology, anthropology, economics, and others).
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Prisons and Public Education
allCourses.description: Looks at the connections between schools and prisons in the United States. Students learn about ideas that push beyond common trope of the “school to prison pipeline.”.

allCourses.title: The Black Protest Tradition
allCourses.restriction: Upper-division students only.
allCourses.description: History and discourses of the black protest tradition. Traces emergence of black protest against racial slavery and white supremacy from the early colonial period to present and the complex elaboration of identity politics within black communities in the twentieth century.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.

allCourses.title: Seminar in African American Studies
allCourses.description: Explores theoretical and methodological issues in Black Studies via concentrated work on a specific ensemble of questions. Emphasis is on generating student responses to the material covered through oral and written reports.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Directed Group Study
allCourses.description: Special topics through directed reading. Paper required.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit for 24 units.

allCourses.title: Independent Study
allCourses.description: Investigation of special topics through directed reading. Paper required.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: University Teaching
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Limited to teaching assistants.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: African American Studies I
allCourses.description: Discusses main contours of African American experience from the forced importation of Africans into the Americas in the late fifteenth century to the development of social movements in post-emancipation societies of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

allCourses.title: African American Studies II
allCourses.description: Introduction to the history of modern racial thinking in Western society and its relationship to the material contexts of racial oppression, with emphasis on its development in British colonies and U.S.

allCourses.title: African American Studies III
allCourses.description: Introduction to theories of racial blackness in the modern world, with emphasis on developments in British colonies and U.S. Traces emergence of blackness as term of collective identity, social organization, and political mobilization.

allCourses.title: Introductory Topics in African American Studies
allCourses.description: Introduction to a broad range of topics in African American studies, exploring history, literature, art, culture, politics, and contemporary social issues. Topical organization of courses addresses issues that have been of importance historically and are reshaping the African diaspora today.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Research in Anatomy
allCourses.description: Individual research supervised by a particular faculty member.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Research in Anatomy and Neurobiology for First-Year Students
allCourses.description: Independent research within the laboratories of graduate training faculty in the Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology for first-year Ph.D. students.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times.

allCourses.title: Human Gross Anatomy
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Study and dissection of the human body, including muscular, skeletal, nervous, and cardiovascular systems. Emphasis on both normal and abnormal structure and function.

allCourses.title: Human Neuroscience
allCourses.description: Study of the human nervous system at the systems level including the physiology and anatomy of sensory, motor, and integrative functions.

allCourses.title: Human Microscopoic Anatomy
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Lecture and laboratory course on human microscopic anatomy. Emphasis is on functional implications of structure of cells and tissues.

allCourses.title: Human Microscopoic Anatomy
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Lecture and laboratory course on human microscopic anatomy. Emphasis is on functional implications of structure of cells and tissues.

allCourses.title: Tutorial in Anatomy
allCourses.description: Series of tutorials on advanced topics in anatomy.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Neuroanatomy
allCourses.description: Exploration of special topics in neuroanatomy.  Primarily library work, but study of prepared slides also included.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Tutorial in Microanatomy
allCourses.description: Special topics in microanatomy.  Primarily library work, but study of prepared histological slides and photographs included.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Systems Neuroscience
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only. Neurobiology and Behavior Majors only.
allCourses.description: Study of the mammalian nervous system at the systems level. Anatomy and physiology of sensory, motor, and integrative functions.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times.

allCourses.title: Epilepsy as a Window to Mechanisms of Neuronal Plasticity
allCourses.description: Understanding the mechanisms of brain disorders provides novel insights into the normal function of neurons and circuits. Discusses approaches to studying mechanisms of brain function ranging from imaging, the use of models and others to study epilepsy.

allCourses.title: Current Topics in Neuroscience
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Focuses on critical reading, presentation, and discussion of current literature in neuroscience research.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Current Topics in Neuroscience
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Focuses on critical reading, presentation, and discussion of current literature in neuroscience research.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Current Topics in Neuroscience
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Focuses on critical reading, presentation, and discussion of current literature in neuroscience research.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Topics in Translational Neuroscience
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only. Interdepartmental Neuroscience Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: One-hour seminar presentation by participating faculty or guest lecturer and open to the science community, followed by one-hour student discussion of the lecture topic or related topic. Students are responsible for presentations and readings.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Molecular, Cellular, & Developmental Neurobiology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Molecular aspects of the structure and function of neurons and glia including neurotransmission, synaptic modulation, and channels.  Neural development at the cellular and molecular level including neurogenesis, pattern formation, trophic factors, axonal growth, and synaptic rearrangement.

allCourses.title: Topics in Neural Circuit Mapping
allCourses.description: Presentations/lectures by invited faculty and student discussion.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Scientific Communication
allCourses.description: Small group meetings for graduate students to practice scientific writing, debate, and presentation skills.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Scientific Communication
allCourses.description: Small group meetings for graduate students to practice scientific writing, debate, and presentation skills.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Ethnography and Anthropological Methods
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Medical Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Anthropological research, learning ethnographic methods, and how to choose a research topic, construct research questions, explore library resources, collect data, and write an analytical paper on research findings.

allCourses.title: Anthropology Careers
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors only. Anthropology Minors only. Medical Anthropology Minors only.
allCourses.description: Gives students the skills and perspective needed to leverage undergraduate anthropology education in diverse career domains. Students explore different career domains (health care, tech development, environmental governance, etc.) and learn to represent themselves professionally.

allCourses.title: Probability and Statistics
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Sociology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: An introduction to probability and statistics. Emphasis on a thorough understanding of the probabilistic basis of statistical inference. Emphasizes examples from sociology, anthropology, and related social science disciplines.

allCourses.title: Probability and Statistics
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Sociology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: An introduction to probability and statistics. Emphasis on a thorough understanding of the probabilistic basis of statistical inference. Emphasizes examples from sociology, anthropology, and related social science disciplines.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ECON 10A OR PSYCH 10A OR ANTHRO 10A OR SOCIOL 10A OR SOC SCI 10A )

allCourses.title: Probability and Statistics
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Sociology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: An introduction to probability and statistics. Emphasis on a thorough understanding of the probabilistic basis of statistical inference. Emphasizes examples from sociology, anthropology, and related social science disciplines.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ECON 10B OR PSYCH 10B OR ANTHRO 10B OR SOCIOL 10B OR SOC SCI 10B ) AND ( ECON 10A OR PSYCH 10A OR ANTHRO 10A OR SOCIOL 10A OR SOC SCI 10A )

allCourses.title: Kinship and Social Organization
allCourses.description: Organization of social life primarily in preindustrial societies. Theories of kinship, marriage regulations, sexual behavior, and social roles. Comparisons of biological, psychological, sociological, and economic explanations of social organization.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.

allCourses.title: Cross-Cultural Studies of Gender
allCourses.description: Explores the construction of gender in national and transnational contexts. Special attention is given to how race, sexuality, class, and global inequalities shape different experiences of gender, and how gender structures political, institutional, and social life across the world.

allCourses.title: Urban Anthropology
allCourses.description: Cultural roles of cities and the processes of urbanization in a comparative perspective. Focus includes nonwestern, nonindustrial societies of past and present; the relationship between modern urban centers across different world regions. Themes covered include: inequality, race, migration, poverty, capitalism.

allCourses.title: Gold: The Alchemy of Socio-Economic Practice
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Archaeology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Economics Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Economics Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Before bitcoin, before derivatives and mortgage-backed securities, before even writing itself, there was gold. Explore gold’s role in the development of culture, politics, and power. From Pharaohs to modern financial wizards, gold has impacted and mediated social life.

allCourses.title: Anthropology of Debt
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Archaeology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Economics Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Economics Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Explores how debt has shaped culture across varied contexts geographically and historically. In what ways have societies naturalized indebtedness, taken it for granted as a fact of life, and used it for organizing social relations.

allCourses.title: Economic Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Economics Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Quantitative Economics Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Business Economics Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Economic systems in comparative perspective: production, distribution, and consumption in market and non-market societies; agricultural development in the third world.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: One course in general science, anthropology, economics, geography, or sociology.

allCourses.title: Ecological Anthropology
allCourses.description: Studies relationships between human communities and their natural environments. The role of environment in shaping culture; effects of extreme environments on human biology and social organization; anthropologist's role in studying global environmental problems, e.g., African famine, tropical rain forests destruction.

allCourses.title: Environmental Anthropology
allCourses.description: Introduces students to anthropological and qualitative research on the relationship of humans, non-humans, and environments. Focuses on how to analyze and evaluate social and cultural differences in environmental perception, relations, justice, governance, sustainability, and cosmology.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ANTHRO 2A or ANTHRO 2B or ANTHRO 2C or ANTHRO 2D

allCourses.title: Humans and Other Animals
allCourses.description: Explores peoples' relationships with other animals, a topic that continues to shape anthropological understandings of humanness, culture, and the social.  Subthemes: symbol and matter, nature/culture, ontologies, relations, moralities, ecologies, futures.

allCourses.title: Immigration, Nation, and Media
allCourses.description: Examines media shapes and reflects public opinion on immigration and its representation of immigrants, citizens, and ideas about the nation, and who belongs and who is a potential threat; as well as the relationship between scholars and journalists.

allCourses.title: Transnational Migration
allCourses.description: Examines the movement of people across national borders, governmentality and the role of state practices to control populations, and issues of citizenship, belonging, and identity. Examples are drawn from the United States, Europe, Latin America, Asia, and Africa.

allCourses.title: Arabs and Muslims in the US
allCourses.description: Offers a critical academic study of Islam in America, focusing on the core tenets of belief, the diversity of practices, and historical transformations that have taken place since the arrival of Muslims in the United States.

allCourses.title: Cultures of the Middle East
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: The diversity of cultures and peoples who constitute the Middle East demonstrates the failure of much contemporary media and discourse to understand this region. Students learn about the broad scope of the contemporary Middle East through an ethnographic lens.

allCourses.title: Elite Cultures
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: The distinctive contribution that ethnographic studies have made to the understanding of elites past and present, in particular societies and globally.

allCourses.title: Controversies, Courts, Cultures: The Anthropology of Law
allCourses.description: Assesses the contributions anthropology has made to legal scholarship, reviewing historical and contemporary themes. Considers both comparative questions of law’s norms, structures, and practices around the globe, and the specific insights anthropology offers about contemporary U.S. law.

allCourses.title: Law and Modernity
allCourses.description: The rise and spread of Enlightenment legal traditions, social contract theory, individual rights, ideologies of "liberty, equality, fraternity"; contradictions of liberal law, its understandings of "primitive" and "civilized"; pervasive myths of property, difference, race, and rights. Reading- and writing-intensive.

allCourses.title: Anthropology of Law
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Criminology, Law and Society Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Social Ecology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Introduces the anthropological study of law through a focus on the foundations of this subfield, its primary methodologies, and several important topics of inquiry, including policing, immigration, and structural inequalities. Provides an international perspective on law and society.

allCourses.title: Science, Technology, Controversy
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors only.
allCourses.description: Explores ways in which the social sciences conceive of science as a sociocultural practice. Emphasis on literature in Science and Technology Studies (STS), especially writings that concern the relationship of science to space and place, power, and politics.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ANTHRO 2A OR ANTHRO 2B OR ANTHRO 2C OR ANTHRO 2D )

allCourses.title: Race, Gender, and Science
allCourses.description: Perfect for pre-health, science, and social science majors wanting to appreciate how science and society interact. Race and gender as biological and socio-cultural constructs are examined. Questions explored: What is disease? What is science? What are social and biological differences.

allCourses.title: Digital Cultures
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Explores cultural and political implications of the infotech revolution and the ways new media are used around the world, new cultural practices and spaces (e.g., cybercafes), debates surrounding the meanings of these new technologies, and their implications for transforming society.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ANTHRO 2A and (ANTHRO 2B or ANTHRO 2C or ANTHRO 2D)

allCourses.title: Special Topics: Social and Economic Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Studies in selected areas of Social and Economic Anthropology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Psychological Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Psychology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Cultural differences and similarities in personality and behavior.  Child-rearing practices and consequent adult personality characteristics, biocultural aspects of child development and attachment, culture and behavior evolutionary models, politically linked personality, cognitive anthropology, psychology of narrative forms, comparative national character studies.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( PSYCH 7A OR ANTHRO 2A OR PSY BEH 9 OR AP PSYCHOLOGY OR ( ( PSYCH 9C OR PSY BEH 11C ) AND ( PSYCH 9B OR PSY BEH 11B ) AND ( PSYCH 9A OR PSY BEH 11A ) ) )

allCourses.title: Medical Anthropology
allCourses.description: Introduces students to cross-cultural perspectives and critical theories in anthropological studies of medicine. Special attention is given to diverse ways of understanding bodies, illnesses, and therapeutic practices in our changing world.

allCourses.title: Cultures of Biomedicine
allCourses.description: An introduction to the anthropolobical study of biomedicine and biotechnology.  Topics include medicalization, experimentation and discovery, diagnosis, expertise, health activism, and biotechnology.

allCourses.title: Medicine, Food, and Health
allCourses.description: With anthropological studies of edible things as its foundation, this course explores topics related to the relationship between medical knowledge, eating, and health from a medical anthropological perspective.

allCourses.title: Anthropology of the Body
allCourses.description: Examines human bodies as both biological and sociocultural entities and explores the relationship among mind, body, and society cross-culturally. Topics include embodiment; race, sex, gender, and the body; somatization; control of the body; commodified bodies; and hybrid/cyborg bodies.

allCourses.title: HIV/AIDS in a Global Context
allCourses.description: Examines issues concerning cultural conceptions of HIV infection and disease worldwide. Topics include treatment and prevention, identity and behavior, risk, ethnicity, gender, youth, sexuality, activism, drug use, illness, religion, the clinical encounter, national belonging, and the pharmaceutical industry.

allCourses.title: Anthropology of Food
allCourses.description: Examines how food communicates ideas about ethnocentrism, disgust, privilege, gender, race, labor, social identities and hierarchies, globalization, power, and the "Western diet" and its health consequences.

allCourses.title: Comics and Medicine
allCourses.description: Patients, caregivers, and healers have increasingly described their illness experiences in comics format, offering therapeutic value for both producers and readers. Read and analyze comics about disability, chronic and mental illness, epidemics, caregiving, dementia, cancer, and health justice.

allCourses.title: Disease, Health, and Inequality
allCourses.description: Examines the relationships among disease, health, and social inequality in the U.S. and globally. Topics include infectious and chronic disease case studies, health policy, and strategies for promoting health equity.

allCourses.title: Nationalism and Ethnicity in the Contemporary World
allCourses.description: An exploration of the concepts of identity, culture, ethnicity, race, and nation through ethnographic cases, with a view to asking larger questions: how do people create nativeness and foreignness? How does "culture" get worked into contemporary racisms and nationalisms.

allCourses.title: History of Anthropological Theory
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Provides foundational knowledge in the discipline of anthropology by reviewing competing approaches in anthropological theory, from the nineteenth century to the present. Covers historically fundamental approaches—social evolutionism, functionalism—and recent movements such as feminism, cultural studies, poststructuralism, and postmodernism.

allCourses.title: Conflict Resolution in Cross-Cultural Perspective
allCourses.description: Examines theories of conflict management. Analyzes how conflict is mitigated in diverse cultures: at the interpersonal level, between groups, and on the international scale. Students discuss readings, hear from conflict management practitioners, and simulate negotiations.
allCourses.same_as: POL SCI 154G, SOC SCI 183E, INTL ST 183E.

allCourses.title: Colonialism and Gender
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: An anthropological enquiry into the ways colonial relations of power have been structured and gendered throughout the world, and to what effect. Examines the social locations of men and women in the everyday exercise of colonial and imperial power.

allCourses.title: The Woman and the Body
allCourses.description: Probes culture and politics of the female body in contemporary American life. Focusing on "feminine beauty," examines diverse notions of beauty, bodily practices, and body politics embraced by American women of different classes, ethnicities, and sexualities.

allCourses.title: Prisons and Public Education
allCourses.description: Looks at the connections between schools and prisons in the United States. Students learn about ideas that push beyond common trope of the “school to prison pipeline.”.

allCourses.title: Special Topics in Cultural and Psychological Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Studies in selected areas of Cultural and Psychological Anthropology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Sex and Conquest in Latin America
allCourses.description: Competing ideas of masculinity and femininity, sexual violence, sexual identities, and gendered hierarchies informed how the Spanish engaged in military and religious domination of Mexican and Andean communities, as well as the forms of native resistance throughout colonial Latin America.

allCourses.title: Ancient Civilization of Mexico and the Southwest
allCourses.description: The prehistory and cultural evolution of the civilization which originated in Mexico, including the Olmecs, Aztecs, Toltecs, Maya, and Zapotec, as well as the Pueblos of the Southwestern U.S. Topics include the origins of food production and of the state.

allCourses.title: Consumption and Culture
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Our modern "society of the spectacle" often equates your consumption to your very humanity. Explores the ways in which our desire for things expresses our identity, politics, place within society, and how what we consume dominates social life.

allCourses.title: Egyptomania
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Archaeology Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: An exploration into the archaeological heritage and cultures of ancient Egypt. Also examines how ancient Egypt became appropriated as a popular cultural phenomenon and site of scholarship in the centuries after the Pharaohs.

allCourses.title: Archaeology of the Islamic World
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Archaeology Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: The archaeological record connected with the Islamic tradition spans nearly 1,500 years and stretches from Spain to South East Asia. Working with artifacts and other materials, students learn about the sites and historical transformations associated with Islam and Muslim societies.

allCourses.title: Archaeology, Politics, and Identity
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. Anthropology Minors have first consideration for enrollment. Archaeology Minors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Archaeologists don’t excavate in a political vacuum. Their research has profound consequences for the ways in which people identify with and claim their cultural heritage. Examines archaeology’s role in constructing such identities through the traces of the past.

allCourses.title: I Dig UCI
allCourses.description: An introduction to archaeological fieldwork through participation in an active excavation on campus. Students engage with research design and learn the foundational methods of archaeological recovery: survey, mapping, sampling strategies, documentation, excavation, artifact identification, and interpretation.

allCourses.title: Special Topics in Archaeology
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Studies in selected areas of Archaeology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Language and Social Cognition
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Explores the relationship between language and cognition in social and cultural contexts. The overall goal is to think through how language structure and use impact how individuals perceive, think about, and understand the world around them.

allCourses.title: Improvisation, Language, and Culture
allCourses.restriction: Upper-division students only.
allCourses.description: Addresses improvisation, both in performance and in everyday life. Examines improvisation as the "flexible regulation" of everyday behavior by exploring different scholarly treatments of language and interaction, and working on developing actual theatrical improvisation skills.

allCourses.title: Language Origins: Evolution, Genetics, and the Brain
allCourses.description: Examines how human language(s) may have originated. Studies pertinent techniques (reconstruction) and addresses related questions, including is our language faculty inborn (i.e., genetically encoded)? Can brain imaging and population genetics research help to unlock this mystery of human evolution?.

allCourses.title: Peoples and Cultures of Latin America
allCourses.description: Surveys the prehistory of Latin America and its indigenous cultures, emphasizing the impact of colonial rule, capitalism, and 20th-century transformations.  Emphasis on communities from several countries. In some years, emphasis on comparisons between the Latin American and Caribbean experiences.

allCourses.title: Indian North America
allCourses.description: A survey of indigenous peoples in North America: American Indians, Alaska Natives, First Nations, Native Americans. Tribal populations and geographic distributions, political and social organization, sovereignty, self-determination, intergovernmental relations; cultural continuity and change; management, preservation, development of environments/resources.

allCourses.title: Race and Empire in Colonial Latin America
allCourses.description: Explores how native people of Latin America with enslaved and free African incorporated and defied Spanish and Portuguese colonization. Focuses on religious adaptions, resistance movements, legal systems, and the emergence of multicultural communities to explain how race shaped European empires.

allCourses.title: Anthropology of the United States
allCourses.description: Examines anthropological research in and of the United States. Topics include race, class, identity, politics, law, and media.

allCourses.title: Peoples of the Pacific
allCourses.description: The cultural history and recent developments among the Pacific peoples of Polynesia, Micronesia, Melanesia, New Guinea, and Australia.

allCourses.title: 21st Century Africa
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Comparative studies of the cultures and societies of Sub-Saharan Africa, with emphasis on critical study of colonialism and postcoloniality, social transformation, and the politics of identity.

allCourses.title: Peoples and Cultures of Post-Soviet Eurasia
allCourses.description: Examines the cultures and political conflicts of the more than 130 indigenous ethnic groups in the European and Asian territories of the former U.S.S.R. Emphasis is on the theoretical issues of ethnicity, nationalism, and conflict management.

allCourses.title: Modern Iran: Cinema and the City
allCourses.description: Exploring modern Iran through film, literature, photography, travel writing, and philosophy and social science texts that introduce students to important concepts in post-colonial studies, social thought, war culture, religion, and media as experienced through the paradigm of a non-Western modernity.

allCourses.title: Special Topics in Area Studies
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Studies in selected areas of Anthropology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors only.
allCourses.description: Anthropological theory designed especially for majors in Anthropology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 3 times as topics vary.

allCourses.description: Senior thesis with Anthropology faculty.

allCourses.description: Field study with Anthropology faculty.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.description: Directed study with Anthropology faculty.

allCourses.description: Independent research with Anthropology faculty.

allCourses.title: Proseminar in Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Year-long intensive introduction to the history of anthropological thought and reading in classical and contemporary ethnography for first-year graduate students.

allCourses.title: Proseminar in Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Year-long intensive introduction to the history of anthropological thought and reading in classical and contemporary ethnography for first-year graduate students.

allCourses.title: Proseminar in Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Year-long intensive introduction to the history of anthropological thought and reading in classical and contemporary ethnography for first-year graduate students.

allCourses.title: Proseminar in Medicine, Science, and Technology
allCourses.restriction: Students pursuing a Graduate Certification in Anthropoligies of Medicine, Science, and Technology have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Explores the phenomena studied by "medical anthropology" and "science and technology studies" are inextricably linked, and how understanding formations requires moving between disparate fields of inquiry.  Required for students pursuing a Graduate Certificate in Anthropoligies of Medicine, Science, and Technology.

allCourses.title: People, Cultures, and Environmental Sustainability
allCourses.description: Anthropological consideration of global environmental sustainability from the perspective of human cultures and communities. Causes and consequences of population growth, natural resource management, environmental law, environmental ethics. Case studies emphasize tropical rain forests, arid lands of Africa and North America.

allCourses.title: Ethnographic Methods
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Exposes students to diverse methods, both traditional and experimental, used in anthropological ethnographic research. Students gain experience practicing diverse methods, and learn to select methods appropriate to particular study designs and contexts.

allCourses.title: Research Design
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Introduces research design for anthropology, including concept work and mapping, research topic and aims development, research question construction, and fieldwork planning.

allCourses.title: Grant and Proposal Writing
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Focuses on production, critique, and revision of student research proposals. A practical seminar designed to improve student proposals, help students through the application processes, and increase students' chances of obtaining support for their research.

allCourses.title: Ethnography and its Collaborative Futures
allCourses.description: Structured readings of selected career-making ethnographic works, past and present, with an emphasis on how ethnographic projects evolve into diverse, collaborative projects.

allCourses.title: Ethnography
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Explores the theory and practice of ethnography with a focus on anthropology, the discipline most associated with ethnography. Students are exposed to the theoretical underpinnings of ethnographic work, traditional and innovative practices, and sample ethnographies.

allCourses.title: Transnational Migration
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Examines borders and boundaries as material and semiotic constructs. Drawing upon an array of literatures, but loosely situated in U.S. geo/biopolitics, explores transformative troublings of places, spaces, borders, and bodies of all sorts.

allCourses.title: Economic Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Classic and contemporary theory in economic anthropology. Case studies: Latin America (primarily Mexico and the Andes), Africa, and the Pacific. Substantive topics: non-market exchange, markets and marketplaces, households, gender, management of common property (fisheries, pastoral lands, forests), labor, and development.

allCourses.title: Seminar in Political Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Explores anthropological approaches to politics. Covers a range of issues and topics, including: theories of culture, power, and hegemony; approaches to colonial and post-colonial relations of global inequality; and ethnographic approaches to the modern state.

allCourses.title: Feminist Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Examines feminist anthropology’s rise as an interdisciplinary field. Paying special attention to issues of power, subjectivity, and authority in the research encounter, feminist anthropologists’ major contributions to ethnography, gender studies, queer studies, and cultural anthropology are surveyed.

allCourses.title: Capital and Empire
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Examines theories of capital and empire via anthropological theory, post/colonial critique, feminist theory, and Black political thought. Moreover, it examines social movements, geo/political trajectories and formations, and political economic trends that have emerged after the 2008 financial crisis.

allCourses.title: Structuralism and Post-Structuralism
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Traces recent theoretical discussions and arguments over the philosophical and historical "subject" from structuralist decenterings toward the characteristically "post-structuralist" contemporary concern with the historical and political constitution of subjectivities and subject positions.

allCourses.title: Humanism and Posthumanism
allCourses.description: Examines alternative forms of human, humanisms, and posthumanisms to explore the inherent ambiguities and shifting boundaries of knowing and being human, and to venture into modes of analysis that problematize the universality and globality of liberal humanism.

allCourses.title: The Cultural Politics of Visual Representation
allCourses.description: Develops a theoretical framework for analyzing and reading visual images. Images, as cultural productions, are steeped in the values, ideologies, and taken-for-granted beliefs of the culture which produced them and a political economy that is class, race, and gender inflected.

allCourses.title: Queer Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Explores historical and contemporary scholarship that employs ethnographic approaches to address the discursive construction of sexuality. Also examines how the discipline of anthropology has been shaped by the study of sexuality.

allCourses.title: Design, Aesthetics, and Social Life
allCourses.description: Anthropology has only recently recognized that design demands consideration as a cultural form linked to, yet nonetheless distinct from, other aesthetic endeavors. Course is largely oriented toward collaboratively working out a conceptual basis for a distinctly anthropological approach to design.

allCourses.title: Digital Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Examines “the digital” from an anthropological perspective by exploring ethnographic research on digital culture and using anthropological frameworks to approach the digital and the human. Readings are interdisciplinary, including work from history and communications.

allCourses.title: Disability Worlds
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Explores disability from a range of methodological and theoretical perspectives. Examines the genealogy of disability in anthropology and related disciplines, with an emphasis on ethnographic work. Topics addressed include access, embodiment, politics, selfhood, and sexuality.

allCourses.title: Ethnographies of Technology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Surveys current ethnographic research pertaining to technologies, technical systems, and infrastructures.

allCourses.title: Secrecy, Security, and Surveillance
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Explores secrecy and security as fundamental to constructions of public and private domains, relations of citizenship and sovereignty, the militarization of everyday life, and the ways that the fabrics of societies are woven of both trust and deceit.

allCourses.title: Natures and Environments
allCourses.description: Examines social scientific understandings of natural contexts and human milieus via a survey of key analytic categories. Begins by examining historical and ongoing definitions and problems organized around “nature” and “environment” as separate but imbricated concepts.

allCourses.title: Dissertation Writing Seminar
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Intended for advanced, post-fieldwork Anthropology graduate students. Emphasis on the presentation of research design and results, problems of ethnographic writing, and qualitative and quantitative data and analysis. Prerequisites: post-fieldwork; graduate standing in Anthropology or consent of instructor.

allCourses.title: Environmental Injustice
allCourses.description: Explores how pollution, climate change, and other environmental problems impact people around the world, often worsening social inequality. Students use social science frameworks to understand environmental problems, different interpretations of these problems, and how people have organized for political change.

allCourses.title: Critical Medical Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Reading-intensive graduate seminar offers an overview of theoretical and ethnographic approaches to illness and healing in different settings, while also studying the political economic distribution of risks that contribute to disease. Students develop their own research papers integrating course readings.

allCourses.title: Anthropology of the Mind
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Reading-intensive graduate seminar looks at emergence of mind/soul in modern age and similar concepts across cultural and historical contexts; studies psychiatric anthropological approaches to trauma, the subconscious, dreaming, madness. Students develop their own research papers integrating course readings.

allCourses.title: Special Topics in Anthropology
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Studies in selected areas of Anthropology. Topics addressed vary each quarter.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.title: Dissertation Research
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Dissertation research with Anthropology faculty.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Independent Study
allCourses.restriction: Graduate students only.
allCourses.description: Independent research with Anthropology faculty.
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.title: Introduction to Sociocultural Anthropology
allCourses.description: Introduction to cultural diversity and the methods used by anthropologists to account for it. Family relations, economic activities, politics, gender, and religion in a wide range of societies. Stresses the application of anthropological methods to research problems.

allCourses.title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology
allCourses.description: Evolutionary theory and processes, comparative primate fossil record, human variation, and the adequacy of theory, and empirical data.

allCourses.title: Introduction to Archaeology
allCourses.description: Archaeological theory and cultural processes with emphasis on the American Southwest, Mesoamerica, and Mesopotamia.

allCourses.title: Introduction to Language and Culture
allCourses.description: Explores what the study of language can reveal about ourselves as bearers of culture. After introducing some basic concepts, examines how cultural knowledge is linguistically organized and how language might shape our perception of the world.

allCourses.title: Global Issues in Anthropological Perspective
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Explores anthropological perspectives on issues of importance in an increasingly global society. Topics include emphases on ethnic conflict; identity; immigration and citizenship; religion and religious diversity; medical anthropology; legal anthropology; development and economic change; gender.

allCourses.title: Visual Anthropology
allCourses.description: Focusing on the construction of culture through visuality, this course engages traditional ethnographic films, popular media and anthropological texts to analyze ethics, “reality” and fiction; propaganda and documentary, construction of a frame, the responsibility of the filmmaker, photographer, and anthropologist.

allCourses.title: Global Cultures and Society
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Majors have first consideration for enrollment. International Studies Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: Offers a general overview of the rise of global interdependence in political, economic, demographic, and cultural terms. Considers what drove people from relative isolation into intensified intercourse with one another, and investigates the consequences of this shift.

allCourses.title: Science, Culture, Power
allCourses.description: Examines science in historical and cultural context (Scientific and Darwinian Revolutions, Manhattan Project, contemporary biosciences) to understand scientific truths and their limits, scientists as social actors, and vital intersections of sciences with religion, politics, gender, and other forms of culture.

allCourses.title: Archaeology or Aliens?: Conspiracy, Pseudoscience, and the Emergence of Civilizations
allCourses.description: Archaeology has inspired (and sometimes actively encouraged) various theories about aliens, lost civilizations, dark conspiracies, and mysterious technologies. Does such an intimate relationship with these fantastic notions undermine archaeology and its claims of authoritative knowledge about past cultures.

allCourses.title: Honors Research Design
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Honors students only.
allCourses.description: Students design a research project and articulate its goals and significance. Written work consists of a research proposal describing the research questions, the relevant literature, methods of data collection and analysis, and ethical considerations.

allCourses.title: Honors Field Research
allCourses.restriction: Anthropology Honors students only.
allCourses.description: Students begin or continue ethnographic field research and gain experience with a variety of data collection methods, including participant-observation, interviews, surveys, and the study of archival and documentary materials.

allCourses.title: Honors Research Analysis
allCourses.description: Students apply qualitative data analysis techniques to ethnographic data collected as part of their Honors research.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ANTHRO H190B and ANTHRO 199. Anthropology Honors ONLY.

allCourses.title: Honors Thesis Writing
allCourses.description: Students draft a senior honors thesis (typically) with the following sections: problem statement, literature review, ethnographic background, and descriptions of the methods, results, and conclusions.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ANTHRO H190C and ANTHRO 199. Anthropology Honors ONLY. Satisfactory completion of the Lower-Division Writing requirement.

allCourses.description: Peer-to-Peer Language Mentor Program in which student mentors work with student mentees to increase the language skills of both participants. One hour weekly meetings. ARABIC 10A is for language mentors.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 4 times.

allCourses.restriction: ARABIC 1A and ARABIC S1AB may not be taken for full credit.
allCourses.description: Designed for students with little or no exposure to Arabic. Using real world texts, provides a firm foundation in the orthography, grammar, syntax, and vocabulary of Modern Standard Arabic. Introduces students to Arab world cultures.

allCourses.title: Introduction to the Koran
allCourses.description: An introduction to understanding the Koran and its significance to Muslim life, culture, and history. An overview of scholarly traditions related to the Koran, and its critics. Close readings of the Koran in English translation.

allCourses.title: Elementary Armenian
allCourses.description: Written and conversational Armenian for students with no knowledge of the language. Students learn the Armenian alphabet, read and comprehend simple texts, and carry basic conversation. Emphasis on reading and comprehension, grammar rules, and basic composition.

allCourses.title: Elementary Armenian
allCourses.description: Continues development of the fundamentals of Armenian, including comprehension, reading of simple texts, basic conversation, and writing with a fair degree of grammatical correctness. Students learn basic reading, writing, and sentence structure through lectures, games, and assignments.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ARMN 1A OR PLACEMENT EXAM or authorization )

allCourses.title: Elementary Armenian
allCourses.description: Focus on building grammatical knowledge of the Armenian language and developing skills in reading, writing, listening, and speaking. Includes a strong emphasis on expanding vocabulary and developing oral proficiency in higher/formal registers.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ARMN 1B. ARMN 1B with a grade of C or better. Placement into ARMN 1C is also accepted.

allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.

allCourses.title: Artists as Writers
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Contemporary art practice involves text, as final form or an integral element. Many contemporary artists consider writing as essential to their practice. Covers historical and contemporary uses of text and image as well as artists' writing.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ART 11A OR ART STU 11A ) AND ( ART 9A OR ART STU 9A ) AND LOWER DIVISION WRITING

allCourses.title: Programming for Artists
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Programming as a means to create interactive artworks with an emphasis on the integration of video, sound, text, and stills. Topics include basic concepts in programming, understanding the limits of code, working with video and audio files, and interface design. Materials fee.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Design for Print
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Investigates the use of print for communication as an artist. Covers the fundamentals of print design and output using digital media.  Materials fee.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Digital Filmmaking Project I
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Students learn to conceive, develop, and produce original video works building directly upon previously learned skills. Use of video stage and post-production editing facilities. Lectures on video/film subjects, production strategies, readings, screening, field trips, and group critiques. Materials fee.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ART 81A OR ART STU 81A ) AND ( ART 81B OR ART STU 81B )

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Performance and the Camera
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Surveys the development of contemporary artists who use performance strategies in the making of videos and films. Students analyze the artist's conceptual approach to performative gestures, actions, and landscapes created for their video or film art.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ART 1B OR ART 91 OR ART 128 OR ART 81A OR ART STU 1B OR ART STU 91 OR ART STU 128 OR ART STU 81A )

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Mechatronic Art I
allCourses.description: Introduces the practice and theory of analog electronics, emphasizing the design and development of simple interactive systems and the integration of such systems into real-world contexts of performance, installation, sculpture, and automated artifacts. Materials fee.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Mechatronic Art III
allCourses.description: As the capstone to the Mechatronic Art series, students develop major projects utilizing electronics, microcontrollers, sensors, and electromechanical devices, in a methodical and supervised context, with technical, design, and aesthetic advice and critique. Materials fee.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ART 65E OR ART 110A OR ART STU 110A )

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: How to be Clever with Stuff
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors have first consideration for enrollment.
allCourses.description: How to Be Clever with Stuff is an introduction to the skilled embodied practices of arts and crafts, working with hand tools, wood, and steel. Class includes technical lecture/demos, short technical assignments, a self-initiated final project, and design drawing. Materials fee.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Writing Nearby
allCourses.restriction: Upper-division students only.
allCourses.description: Art writing is increasingly an area of scholarship unto itself as well as a discursive arm of contemporary art practice. Investigates the politics of art writing as well as training students in its various writing practices.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ART 9A OR ARTSTU 9A ) AND ( ART 11A OR ARTSTU 11A ) AND LOWER DIVISION WRITING

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in Contemporary Painting
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Investigation of issues in modern and contemporary art work and criticism, wherein an assessment of Modernist influences is followed by the examination of contemporary painting as a cross-disciplinary practice employing popular culture, "high art," theory, and new technology.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ART 9A. Recommended: Satisfactory completion of the upper-division writing requirement.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in Contemporary Drawing
allCourses.description: Investigation of drawing as a primary practice rather than a developmental tool. Explores the relationship between Conceptualism, process and content, and considers the historical changes in method, presentation, and theory, from past to present.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Topics in History of Contemporary Art
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Surveys mid-19th and 20th-century art production, from modernity through post-modernity, in a historical and cultural context.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times as topics vary.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Afro-Futurism I
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: First of a two-part course on the futuristic artistic vision of Black film, video, and cyberspace. Deals with critical analyses of the Black image in Western Art history, and its association to contemporary Hip Hop culture, art, and music.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Afro-Futurism II
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Second of a two-part course on the futuristic artistic visions of Black film, video, and cyberspace. Deals with modern techno-culture, digital activism, and designing technology based on African aesthetic principles of contemporary Hip Hop International Culture.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in Media, Violence, and Fear
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Violence has been instrumental in story-telling throughout history in art, literature, religion, and entertainment. Continuing presence of media violence provoked debates among parents, politicians, media producers, and academics. Examines history, theory, aesthetics, economics, and politics of violent representation.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ART 9A. Satisfactory completion of the Upper-Division Writing requirement is recommended.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in Photography
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Rigorous investigation of photographic practices and critical writings, the relationship of photography to the construction and maintenance of cultural institutions, the circulation of photographic ideas in society, and photography and technology.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ART 1A or ART 71A or ART 71B or ART 152A or ART 152B or ART 152C or ART 152D or ART 152E or ART 190B. Recommended: Satisfactory completion of the Upper-Division Writing requirement.
allCourses.repeatability: May be taken for credit 2 times.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in Techno-Arts
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Addresses issues related to artmaking practices that emerge in tandem with new technologies. Topics include sociopolitical contexts of techno-art; utopic/dystopic framings; key moments in the history of techno-arts.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in Experimental Film History
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: A critical study of experimental film/video art genres and production techniques considering their narrative, structural, iconographic, and cultural aspects. Hollywood narrative, Nouvelle Vague, American Independent, and Video Art compared in terms of production innovation, design, and conceptual content.  Materials fee.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Issues in New Genres
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Investigates issues in post-studio practices, including concepts of time, relational aesthetics, site-specificity, institutional critique, and the post-medium condition.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ART 9A. Recommended: Satisfactory completion of the Upper-Division Writing requirement.
allCourses.repeatability: Unlimited as topics vary.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Art, Design, and Electronic Culture
allCourses.description: Introduction to historical and theoretical foundations of digital media art, tracing how information technologies seeded growth of new expressive medium. Considers how today's pervasive digital culture evolved through interdisciplinary collaborations between artists, engineers, scientists, scholars.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Cultural History of the Anthropocene
allCourses.description: A survey of the ongoing interactions between technological and social change through the 19th century and 20th century, with special attention to the history of computing, changing arts and cultural practices, and the idea of the Anthropocene.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Intelligences of Arts
allCourses.description: Introduces contemporary neuroscience and new approaches to cognition – embodied, enactive, extended, situated, distributed. Reviews the history of related  ethological, biological, psychological, technological, and philosophical traditions. Considers arts and cultural practices from these and other perspectives, and considers case studies.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Projects in New Technologies
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Working with media such as electronic still cameras, desktop publishing, faxes, satellites, virtual reality, digitized imaging. Cultural issues pertinent to the emergence of new technology (e.g., ethical concerns, social impact, copyright laws, nontraditional approaches to distribution, cyberpunk, global markets).
allCourses.repeatability: May be repeated for credit unlimited times.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Digital Filmmaking Pre-Production
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Examines the preparatory and planning stages of video production, including script writing, story boarding, location scouting, script breakdown, and budgeting. Projects may encompass one or more of these stages which will be explored through readings, discussions, and demonstrations. Materials fee.

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: Digital Filmmaking Post-Production
allCourses.restriction: Art Majors only.
allCourses.description: Examines procedures and techniques utilized in video production after principal shooting is completed, including effects processing, composting, sound design, and DVD authoring. Projects focus on these processes, and are explored through readings, discussions, and demonstrations. Materials fee.
allCourses.prerequisite_text: ( ART 81A OR ART STU 81A ) AND ( ART 81B OR ART STU 81B )

allCourses.school: Claire Trevor School of the Arts
allCourses.title: The Graphic Novel
